title: Speak, Lord (1 Samuel 3)
hookLine: a boy hears his name at night three times, and finally answers
carry: let none of his words fall to the ground

lines: THE LAMP OF GOD NOT YET OUT.
HERE AM I; FOR THOU CALLEDST ME.
cards: "And the word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision." Precious here means rare. Heaven had gone quiet.

Hannah's son Samuel is now a boy serving the old priest Eli at Shiloh, and one night he's lying down in the temple, where the ark of God is. The lamp of God hasn't gone out yet. Eli's eyes have grown so dim he can't see.
Then a voice calls the boy's name. He runs to the old man: "Here am I; for thou calledst me." Eli sends him back to bed.
It happens a second time, and a third.

teach.h: SAMUEL DID NOT YET KNOW THE LORD.
teach.b: Why does Samuel keep running to the wrong room? The text answers plainly: "Now Samuel did not yet know the LORD, neither was the word of the LORD yet revealed unto him."
He's never heard this voice, so he takes it for the one voice he knows: Eli's.
On the third time, the old man who can barely see is the one who perceives it: "Eli perceived that the LORD had called the child." Eli hasn't restrained his own sons, a scandal in the chapter before.
But tonight he does the one thing a teacher can do.

He gives the boy words: if he calls you, "thou shalt say, Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth." The LORD comes and calls as before, and the boy answers, "Speak; for thy servant heareth." He leaves one word out.
Eli said Speak, LORD. Samuel says only Speak. Some readers have wondered why: nerves, not yet knowing the name, or the text being careful.

teach.h: A HARD WORD FOR ELI'S OWN HOUSE.
teach.b: What comes next is hard: a message of judgment on Eli's own house. In the morning Samuel is afraid to tell him. Eli insists, and when he hears it, says only, "It is the LORD: let him do what seemeth him good."

Then the chapter closes on the boy: the LORD was with him, and let none of his words fall to the ground. A quiet season ends with a child who learned to answer, from a man who knew he was being passed over.

how: Some Christians use Samuel's words, speak, for thy servant heareth, before reading scripture or in quiet prayer, and read 1 Samuel 3 as a story about learning to recognize God's call.

s: Samuel ran to Eli because he hadn't heard the voice clearly
he heard his name. he just did not yet know the LORD (1 Samuel 3:7).
Samuel's answer leaves out a word Eli gave him
Eli said, Speak, LORD. Samuel says, Speak; for thy servant heareth (3:9–10).
Samuel's first message from God was good news for Eli
it was judgment on Eli's house, and Samuel feared to tell him.

games.q: you're Eli, old and nearly blind. the boy has woken you three times saying, here am I, you called me. you didn't. what do you tell him?
o: you're dreaming. go back to sleep.
go lie down. if he calls, say, Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth.
stay here with me, and I'll answer for you.
games.why: Eli perceives that the LORD is calling the child, and gives him the words (1 Samuel 3:8–9), though the message will be against Eli's own house.

practice: Samuel kept answering the voice he already knew, so for a moment set aside the usual voices in your head: the list, the worry, the old arguments.
If you pray, say the boy's words once, quietly, "Speak; for thy servant heareth," and then stop talking; if you don't, simply say to yourself, I'm listening, and let the quiet stay quiet.
Don't hunt for a message; just practice being the one who hears.

wordCard.voice: Speak. The boy Samuel's answer in the night at Shiloh, after three calls and an old priest's help: speak; for thy servant heareth.
